report:
**Conclusion:** Probiotics appear to produce **small, adjunctive improvements in glucose control in type 2 diabetes—most consistently fasting plasma glucose**—but they should **not** be viewed as a stand-alone treatment or replacement for diet, exercise, metformin, or other prescribed therapy. A 28-RCT meta-analysis (n=1,947) found benefit mainly for fasting glucose, with larger effects in poorly controlled diabetes and people not using insulin; adverse-event reporting was incomplete (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8166562/). A 2023 RCT meta-analysis similarly reported reduced fasting blood glucose with low heterogeneity (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12967-023-04306-0). However, a GRADE-style Clinical Nutrition analysis rated evidence **low certainty for HbA1c and fasting glucose** and said HbA1c reductions were not clinically significant (https://www.clinicalnutritionjournal.com/article/S0261-5614(21)00547-1/abstract). A 2024 meta-analysis suggested possible HbA1c/insulin/HOMA-IR benefits depending on treatment duration, but effects were modest (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39114293/).  

**Practical takeaway:** reasonable to discuss as an add-on, but strain, dose, and duration are not standardized; monitor glucose and continue usual care.
